extracted.intended_audience: USFWS biologists, conservation scientists, and legal reviewers preparing or evaluating ESA species status assessments/listing determinations
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluate a species' current and future viability under the Endangered Species Act using the three-part framework of resiliency, representation (adaptive capacity), and redundancy across analysis units, and determine listing status for the whole range or a significant portion of the range. Includes use of climate scenarios and threat-factor analysis to project mid- and late-century conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resiliency (per analysis unit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Population resiliency depends on demographic conditions (including distribution size, population size, and connectivity) and the overall amount and quality of habitat that is available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resiliency is evaluated for each analysis unit using categorical scores (e.g., Low, Low/Moderate, Moderate, Extirpated). Resiliency is largely influenced by the size of population score, as this parameter is the most important in determining resiliency. Specifically, the resiliency score cannot be higher than the size of population score. Debris flows caused by heavy precipitation events (with or without wildfire burn scars) are a primary threat that lowers resiliency by reducing population size and degrading habitat. Connectivity, habitat amount, habitat quality, and demographic distribution are used to assign resiliency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation (adaptive capacity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Representation, or adaptive capacity, is maximized in a species with healthy populations distributed across the breadth of its evolutionary lineages and ecological niches that is capable of moving to new, suitable environments or capable of altering their physical or behavioral traits (phenotypes) to match changing environmental conditions through either plasticity or genetic change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess changes from historical to current conditions in evolutionary lineages and ecological niches. Consider impacts of habitat loss and isolation, disrupted connectivity and limited gene flow (increasing genetic drift and inbreeding), reduced plasticity (e.g., feeding plasticity, thermal tolerance), and whether remaining occupied miles and populations preserve evolutionary potential. Losses of lower-elevation refugial habitats reduce representation by eliminating recolonization pathways.

rubrics_metrics.name: Redundancy (distributional redundancy to withstand catastrophes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Redundancy is the number and distribution of populations from historical to current conditions relative to the magnitude of anticipated catastrophic events, ensuring that multiple populations contribute to species viability since all occurrences are unlikely to be impacted simultaneously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how loss of historically occupied habitats and lower reaches has diminished redundancy. Count occurrences (e.g., 17 extant occurrences across four analysis units) and assess how loss/extirpation of one or more analysis units would reduce redundancy. Consider the role of refugial habitats in protecting from and enabling recovery after catastrophic events and the potential for human interventions (e.g., salvage) to maintain redundancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of future climate/emissions scenarios
rubrics_metrics.description: Future-condition analyses are based on two plausible scenarios using RCP4.5 and RCP8.5 at mid-century (2030-2059) and late-century (2070-2099) to project changes in stream temperature, stream flow, and fire and to assess future threats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply climate model outputs (best available science) to project changes in fire probability/area burned, mean summer/winter stream flows, 10-year flood event magnitudes, and August stream temperatures. Use these projections with other threats to assess future resiliency, representation, and redundancy at mid- and late-century. Rationale for timeframes: model projection reliability and availability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threat-factor analysis under ESA section 4(a)(1)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Act requires determination based on whether a species meets endangered/threatened definitions because of any of the following factors: (A) present or threatened destruction/modification/curtailment of habitat or range; (B) overutilization; (C) disease or predation; (D) inadequacy of existing regulatory mechanisms; (E) other natural or manmade factors affecting continued existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate each factor and the cumulative effects. For this species, habitat loss, degradation, and fragmentation (Factor A) were identified as the most substantial threats. Consider nonnative species, small population effects, and climate change (including debris flows driven by wildfire and heavy precipitation) as contributing threats; none of the identified threats were insignificant enough to exclude from future condition evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination of status throughout all of its range
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine whether a species is endangered or threatened across its entire range, evaluate current threats, cumulative effects, current resiliency/representation/redundancy, and foreseeable future projections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider presence/number/distribution of populations and occupied habitat miles, population stability and reproduction, capacity to withstand stochastic events, connectivity and recolonization ability, and future projections under climate scenarios. Use best available information to conclude whether species is currently in danger of extinction or likely to become so within the foreseeable future.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significant Portion of the Range (SPR) analysis framework
rubrics_metrics.description: A species may warrant listing if it is endangered or likely to become so throughout all or a significant portion of its range. For SPR analysis, both (1) the portion must be significant and (2) the species must be in danger of extinction in that portion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Service may address either the 'status' question or the 'significance' question first. If the first question addressed is negative, the other need not be evaluated for that portion. To evaluate status in a portion, examine whether threats/effects are greater in a biologically meaningful portion than elsewhere. To evaluate significance, consider geographic size relative to range, percentage of occurrences and occupied habitat, and unique biological attributes (e.g., unique genetic alleles, spatial disjunction). Example: two AUs accounting for ~18% of occurrences and <25% of river miles were not found to be individually or collectively significant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categorical scoring of condition parameters
rubrics_metrics.description: Use categorical scores for parameters (Amount of habitat, Quality of habitat, Dispersal/Connectivity, Size of population, and Resiliency) for each analysis unit and timepoint (current, mid-century, late-century).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tables present values as Low, Low/Moderate, Moderate, or Extirpated. Compare parameter scores across AUs and across scenarios/timepoints to determine changes in viability components. Use those scores to inform resiliency/representation/redundancy conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary threats to include in future projections
rubrics_metrics.description: Include habitat loss, habitat degradation, habitat fragmentation, increased risk of wildfire, nonnative species, small population effects, and climate change (extreme precipitation metrics, stream flows, and stream temperatures) as threats projected to influence viability into the future.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat none of the identified threats as insignificant; project their influence using climate models, expert discussions, literature review, and area-specific model aggregation tools (e.g., Cal-Adapt). Consider impacts from recreation, dams, hydrological modifications, mining, and roadways as ongoing human-related threats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of proxies for catastrophic risk (debris flows/floods)
rubrics_metrics.description: Modeled changes in wintertime base flows and the magnitude of 10-year flood events are used as proxies for changes in extreme precipitation/wintertime storms that drive debris flows, which in turn affect resiliency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify changes relative to a modeled baseline (e.g., 1.1–1.9 times higher for 10-year flood events) and interpret higher magnitudes as increased risk of debris flows and population extirpation for occurrences in affected reaches. Use regional breakdown (e.g., Cajon Creek, Santa Ana River Mainstem) to assess AU-specific extirpation risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of recovery potential and management actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether populations or areas have demonstrated natural recolonization after catastrophic events and whether human interventions (e.g., fish salvage) and management decisions can mitigate risks and maintain redundancy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for salvage and restoration potential in redundancy/resiliency judgments. Note that invasive species are hard to eradicate and management choices influence their level of impact. Connectivity, when intact, supports recolonization and can reduce extinction risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal horizons for 'foreseeable future' and model reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreseeable future timeframes used for projections are mid-century (2030-2059) and late-century (2070-2099), representing periods for which reasonably reliable predictions about threats and species responses can be made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose timeframes based on range of available climate model projections used to project stream temperature, stream flow, and fire, and because these model projections are considered the best available science. Evaluate species' response to threats at these timepoints to assess likelihood of becoming endangered within the foreseeable future.
